topStories.bodyText: Auto-grading decade-old Hacker News discussions with hindsight 10 Dec, 2025 There are two macro reasons for why I think the exercise is interesting more generally: I believe it is quite possible and desirable to train your forward future predictor given training and effort. Vibe coding the actual project was relatively painless and took about 3 hours with Opus 4.5, with a few hickups but overall very impressive. The repository is on GitHub here: karpathy/hn-time-capsule . Here is the progression of what the code does: Given a date, download the frontpage of 30 articles For each article, download/parse the article itself and the full comment thread using Algolia API. Package up everything into a markdown prompt asking for the analysis. Here is the prompt prefix I used: Render the results into static HTML web pages for easy viewing Host the html result pages on my website: https://karpathy.ai/hncapsule/ Host all the intermediate results of the data directory if someone else would like to play. It's the file data.zip under the exact same url prefix (intentionally avoiding a direct link). I spent a few hours browsing around and found it to be very interesting. A few example threads just for fun: December 11 2015 original announcement of OpenAI :'). December 22 2015 SpaceX launch webcast: Orbcomm-2 Mission My code (wait, Opus' code?) on GitHub can be used to reproduce or tweak the results. Running 31 days of 30 articles through GPT 5.1 Thinking meant 31 * 30 = 930 LLM queries and cost about $58 and somewhere around ~1 hour. The LLM megaminds of the future might find this kind of a thing a lot easier, a lot faster and a lot cheaper.

items.bodyText: Auto-grading decade-old Hacker News discussions with hindsight 10 Dec, 2025 There are two macro reasons for why I think the exercise is interesting more generally: I believe it is quite possible and desirable to train your forward future predictor given training and effort. Vibe coding the actual project was relatively painless and took about 3 hours with Opus 4.5, with a few hickups but overall very impressive. The repository is on GitHub here: karpathy/hn-time-capsule . Here is the progression of what the code does: Given a date, download the frontpage of 30 articles For each article, download/parse the article itself and the full comment thread using Algolia API. Package up everything into a markdown prompt asking for the analysis. Here is the prompt prefix I used: Render the results into static HTML web pages for easy viewing Host the html result pages on my website: https://karpathy.ai/hncapsule/ Host all the intermediate results of the data directory if someone else would like to play. It's the file data.zip under the exact same url prefix (intentionally avoiding a direct link). I spent a few hours browsing around and found it to be very interesting. A few example threads just for fun: December 11 2015 original announcement of OpenAI :'). December 22 2015 SpaceX launch webcast: Orbcomm-2 Mission My code (wait, Opus' code?) on GitHub can be used to reproduce or tweak the results. Running 31 days of 30 articles through GPT 5.1 Thinking meant 31 * 30 = 930 LLM queries and cost about $58 and somewhere around ~1 hour. The LLM megaminds of the future might find this kind of a thing a lot easier, a lot faster and a lot cheaper.

It's okay if it's not fast. We want to be able to have the weights, and a cli to run them that we can point at a ROM. Apparently Opus found and then used this collection of conformance tests for the NES CPU released 15 years ago by Christopher Pow. items.rawBody: How I Built the Most AI-Pilled Company in the World Don't be put off by the clickbait headline, this piece by Jacob Sansbury describing how they are building Spawn is a fascinating exploration of the bleeding edge of what's possible with agentic engineering against frontier models. Spawn is a massively multiplayer gaming environment where players can use prompts (to the in-game agent, Savi) to modify the game world. I fired it up on my phone for a few minutes and was able to prompt a castle into existence, then a dragon, then ride the dragon to fly around that castle. By Jacob's telling, Spawn is now being developed autonomously by a swarm of Fable-powered agents costing over $3 million in tokens per month ("we spend 30x payroll on AI tokens"). Our agents change the live code directly and ship to production hourly, so they read every error, bug report and metric themselves. About 60% of our work starts from a production error, a Savi bug report (Savi is the AI you build games with in Spawn), something odd in our logs, or a feature request. Savi files bugs herself. When a user hits one, or Savi hits one in the product, she files it. It goes straight to an agent that decides whether it's a real bug to fix, something we won't fix, or intentional design that needs a decision. Usually it becomes a change, delivered to that user within an hour, with a message in the same chat. This is continuous deployment turned up to 11: A loop this tight only works if it never stops, so we treat an hour without a ship as a SEV-0, our most severe kind of incident. Unshipped changes pile up, and every problem already in production lasts longer. The feedback slows down too. An agent can only keep a few hours of work in its head, so shipping faster than that actually helps it stay coherent. [...] We can roll back a broken change in 30 seconds, exactly where it's broken and nowhere else. When a monitor or a log alert fires, it starts or wakes an agent that owns the incident, and we break things on purpose to test that those recovery paths work. My eyebrows raised at least a dozen times reading this. I have trouble imagining this style of development working on software with higher stakes for when something goes wrong, but for a game this appears to be working surprisingly well. Jacob says that Fable 5 (and then 5.1) was the model that made this level of autonomy possible. Opus 5.5 doesn't quite hack it for them, and when they tried GPT-6 Astra to apply fixes from a security review everything stopped working: Every feature had been disabled and marked to be turned on again once the security fixes were done. Astra had gone through our whole product and made the insecure things secure by turning them off. These kinds of extreme experiments are why I'm excited about game development as a substrate for exploring the edges of what today's coding agents can do. Tags: game-design , ai , generative-ai , llms , claude , coding-agents , agentic-engineering , claude-mythos-fable

items.rawBody: GitHub Octoverse 2026 I'm at GitHub Universe today (GitHub gave me a free ticket through their "GitHub Stars" program). EVP Jay Parikh just announced this year's Octoverse report, and highlighted these numbers in particular: This is a pretty stark representation of the impact of agentic engineering on GitHub. In 2026, merged pull requests tripled in less than a year to 220 million per month. Commits more than tripled to 7.38 billion per month, with most of that increase in the second half of this year. New repository rate doubled this year, to 30.3 million per month. The report includes new numbers by industry, and breaks out numbers for repositories that involve "interoperability or reverse engineering". The methodology section includes notes about how they did this: Top countries by pushes to public repositories, adjusted by profile location . Pushes from each country were summed across the Octoverse year. To adjust for biases caused by VPN usage, LLM classification was used to extract the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code from the profiles of GitHub users who contributed pushes during this period [...] Industry . items.rawBody: I've written before about how November 2025 was an inflection point for coding agents - the point where Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1 crossed a tipping point that meant their respective coding agents became reliable daily drivers for software engineers. I think we've reached a new inflection point in October 2026, and this time it's for vibe coding computer games . Tree Appreciator Emberwick Battle Drones Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove Four times as insulting What happens if someone actually puts the work in? You should build a game! Claude Opus 5.5 in particular exhibits meaningful improvements in several areas needed to build a compelling game: 3D modeling Music generation (see Scrimshaw Jukebox ) Game design (!) That last one is particularly important. Models have been able to create something that looks like a game for quite a while now, as seen in my previous experiments . The challenge has been getting to a game that's actually fun to play . Game design is a deep subject area. I won't pretend to be well versed in it - I know enough to have respect for it as a craft. Creating a novel, compelling gameplay loop which challenges players at the right level and provides a satisfying learning curve is a fine art. I didn't think the models could do it. Then I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 to "Make it a LOT more fun"... and it did . In the past few weeks I've vibe coded (in the classic sense of the term - no looking at the code at all) four games that I've genuinely enjoyed playing. I attended Foo Camp in Berkeley over the weekend and met several people who were having similar experiences. Building games that play well is shockingly easy now. The new challenge is coming up with concepts for games that are novel and delightful and that wouldn't exist without AI assistance. I haven't done an exhaustive study, but my current impression is that GPT-6 Astra isn't quite there yet. It can absolutely build a game, but its sense of fun doesn't match that of Opus 5.5. I expect OpenAI will get there by the end of the year. Here are the four game projects that have convinced me that the models are now capable of producing fun games with very little guidance. All four are built in HTML and JavaScript and run entirely in the browser. Tree Appreciator The smallest game I found to be genuinely delightful is Tree Appreciator . I used the regular Claude chat interface for this - it didn't even need Claude Code. I built this on a whim while we were driving along Skyline Boulevard looking at trees. My prompt was: Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful. I've found that telling models to use three.js works really well. Claude doesn't have its own image generation model but is capable of building full-color 3D models that look and feel excellent. This game required no iteration or follow-up prompting at all - I got the game in a single shot. It gave me back a charming little mobile-friendly spot-the-difference game. You can play that here . Here's the chat transcript that built it. It's pleasingly relaxing. The graphics are fun, and collecting trees that you have completed in a "herbarium" provides a nice, cosy sense of accomplishment. Emberwick This was a more ambitious project that I again built using regular Claude chat. I started out by building an experimental prototype of an engine for a top-down fantasy RPG: Build a demo game engine three.js which is a top down (but at an angle) RPG - the player gets to move through the world with one or two companions. Create a fantasy village setting that demonstrates walking around outside and then shows how when the player enters a building the wall between the player and the camera goes transparent so the user can see what is happening Add some NPCs and plenty of furniture and different types of building some with an upstairs - be creative, make it look great Here's that first version . It worked really well! I was inspired to increase my ambitions: Make it not so flat - the buildings are great but the landscape itself is completely flat at the moment, fix that Add basements to two of the buildings with a tunnel system joining them below the village Add the start of a rocky mountain on one side of the village containing a cave with a sleeping troll Here's that version . When that produced a good result, I decided to push it all the way: Now turn this into an actual game - quadruple the size of the playable area, introduce fun game mechanics, add a plot that isn't too cliche, some twists, a magic system, make it really good We're back to prompts like "make it really good" here! Asking for a plot that "isn't too cliche" seemed to work too - it's a bit cliché, but still novel enough that I enjoyed following the story. Unlike Tree Appreciator, this took quite a bit of additional playtesting and prompting to get to a finished version. This was mainly due to gameplay problems - things like a character not being in the right place to complete a quest because a different story element had caused them

items.rawBody: Game Boy Color on My Conference Badge I'm at GitHub Universe this week and, similar to last year , the conference badge is a full-blown color screen computer. I've been hacking around with it again, and then I ran into with Steve Francia... who worked with Gemini to get a full NES emulator working on it, and then went a step further and deployed an emulator for both the Game Boy and the Game Boy Color. Which means, if you can obtain the ROM, you can run The Legend of Zelda: Link's Awakening on your conference badge! A neat feature of the badge is that you can turn it upside down and then use game controller touch buttons that are built into the badge body. items.rawBody: GPT-6.1 Terra It's always interesting to note which aspects of a new model are emphasized in the release announcement. In the case of GPT-6.1 Terra, OpenAI went with visual reasoning and computer use: We’re introducing GPT-6.1 Terra , a fast, efficient model that combines detailed visual reasoning and precise computer use alongside clearer, more natural writing. A significant step up from GPT‑5.6 Terra, it excels at the communication and computer-based tasks that fill the workday, from drafting proposals and interpreting technical drawings to filling out forms and editing videos. Terra sits in the same position as Sonnet in the Anthropic model collection - not the cheapest or the most expensive, making it harder to decide when to use it. Computer use is a good example of a task that benefits from a less expensive model, since you might put it to work on automated, repetitive tasks. OpenAI's Ted Sanders provided some useful advice in a comment on Hacker News: In the case of GPT-6.1 Terra, I'd say Terra is probably better than Astra and Sol at technical communication, similar on vision and computer use (but much faster!), and a bit worse on most other things. For API developers, it's a nice midrange option if you want something cheaper than Sol but a lot smarter than Luna (especially for vision / computer use / communication). For subscribers, it's not a bombshell release - if you're hitting usage limits, maybe it helps you go a bit further, and if you want clearer communication or faster computer use, it can be a nice option to select. Here are the pelicans for the different reasoning levels. This pelican for "max" cost 11.3161 cents and took 4 minutes and 11 seconds: Here's a new comparison grid showing pelicans for every reasoning level of OpenAI's current frontier lineup: GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6.1 Terra, and GPT-6 Luna. GPT-6.1 Terra is priced at $1/million input tokens and $5/million output - almost half the price of GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-6.1 Sol, and around 10x the price of GPT-6 Luna. Via Hacker News Tags: ai , openai , generative-ai , llms , llm-pricing , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , llm-release , gpt , ted-sanders

items.rawBody: Research: webframe: evaluated as a scraper and a sandbox webframe is a neat little project from Jeff Lindsay which lets you "run a web page like a program" - you point it at a URL or file and it executes it in a hidden headless web view and outputs console.log() to standard output and any exceptions to standard error. It's written in Go on top of the glaze library, which provides access to a system browser ("WKWebView on macOS, WebKitGTK on Linux, WebView2 on Windows") so it doesn't need to bundle its own browser engine. It reminds me of my own shot-scraper javascript tool, albeit in a much smaller package that doesn't depend on Playwright. I had Claude Opus 5.5 put it through its paces and prepare a research report for me. Here's the prompt I used: Explore https://github.com/tractordev/webframe try running it and put it though its paces, build a few exploratory prototypes, then evaluate it as a potential sandboxing tool and as a tool for scraping web pages using the same patterns encouraged by the "shot-scraper JavaScript" command (see simonw/shot-scraper on GitHub, docs directory) Tags: browsers , go , javascript , jeff-lindsay , shot-scraper

items.rawBody: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro Kimi K3.1 Pro landed on the Kimi API today - it's not yet open weights, but Moonshot promise "Full model weights will be released by Nov 4, 2026". They're also offering a "Highspeed" version that's 2-3x faster, at twice the price (except for input token cache hits, which are priced the same). The US dollar pricing is $2.00/million tokens for input and $10/million for output - the same as GPT-6.1 Sol and half the price of Claude Opus 5.5. Moonshot's own benchmarks show Kimi as approximately level with Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra - beating them on a few benchmarks, coming close on others. Artificial Analysis scored Kimi at 55 - ahead of Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra, and Gemini 4 Argon (all at 53) and behind only Claude Opus 5.5 (58). This is the first time a (soon-to-be) open weight model has scored this highly against the frontier. I tried it out via the Moonshot API using the llm openai endpoint command I added to LLM 0.32 back in August: llm openai endpoint \ https://api.moonshot.ai/v1 \ --key kimi \ -m kimi-k3.1-pro \ "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" \ --responses \ -o reasoning_effort low \ > kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stdout.txt \ 2> kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stderr.txt llm openai endpoint can run prompts against any OpenAI-compatible endpoint but doesn't log the results, hence the extra options to save stdout and stderr (the reasoning trace). Here are the pelicans I got for Kimi K3.1 Pro on the three reasoning levels it supports - low, medium, and max. This is max: For comparison, I ran fresh pelicans against Kimi K3 on those three reasoning levels. Via Hacker News Tags: ai , generative-ai , llms , llm , llm-pricing , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , llm-release , ai-in-china , moonshot , kimi

items.rawBody: Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security If you're running anything on PHP it's vital you upgrade - today's updates (across the entire PHP 8.x line) address two remote code execution holes, and there have been exploits circulating since last night, thanks to a leak in the coordinated disclosure process. This post from the PHP Foundation explain what went so wrong: On Tuesday, October 20th, at around 15:00 UTC, the two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media. They came with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2). No technical details leaked. In response, the PHP project brought its pre-announcement forward and published it at 19:30 UTC . It also moved the release from October 22nd, 14:00 UTC, to October 21st, 14:00 UTC [...] As a result of the leak and pre-announcement around 20:00 UTC, Calif, one of the security firms that had reported the issues mistakenly published a video. It showed their proof of concept working against a number of targets and revealed a few additional, though limited, details about the vulnerabilities. Copies of the deleted video started circulating on social media soon after. items.rawBody: My latest vibe coded game experiment is a Command & Conquer style RTS (Real Time Strategy) game called Battle Drones ( play it here ). Unlike my previous experiments , this one is actually fun to play . I'm somewhat embarrassed to admit that I got there by telling Claude to "Make it a LOT more fun". It also supports multiplayer between nearby devices using audio to synchronize game state! Here's what I've built so far, and some of the things I learned along the way. Battle Drones How I built this v1: the initial prototype v2: full sprites v3: varied terrain v4: the fun update v5: Battle Drones goes 3D v8: Archipelago v10: Goliath, and agent battles Agent battles v11: Random Maps v12: Multiplayer via sound Some thoughts Update: Online multiplayer support Battle Drones My initial goal was to build an RTS game I could play on my phone, in the style of Command & Conquer . I have fond memories of the 1995 original (I liked Red Alert too) and wanted to recapture a little bit of the magic. After 12 major iterations (and 321 commits by coding agents, mainly Claude Code) I now have a browser-based game that works on mobile and desktop, has multiple play modes, several maps (including a random map generator) and even supports multiplayer for two devices within microphone range of each other. ( Update : also online multiplayer ; the audio multiplayer induced headaches!) Here's a video demo of Battle Drones running in a desktop browser: Features so far include: 9 buildings, 7 ground vehicles, 6 aerial vehicles, 3 infantry units - all 3D models, which you can browse here Fog of war Different weapons are needed to target aerial or ground vehicles Six maps , across five biomes - temperate, desert, arctic, volcanic, tropical A random map generator Skirmish mode - red vs. blue on a rotationally symmetrical map Last Stand mode - one player holds out against as many waves of enemies as possible Area effect weapons: Barrage, EMP, Drop Pod, Sky Hammer Crate drops with bonus resources In-game music that responds to events - it gets more intense as fighting breaks out Different in-game AI personalities (Balanced, Rush, Air Swarm, Boom, Skyforce, Ironclad) AI vs. AI mode, to watch those personalities play each other The Goliath - a giant stomping mech with laser eyes and arm cannons and the ability to establish a new base Mutators that add extra rules or twists A "Daily Op" challenge Ranks and achievements ( Medals ) Agent vs. Agent mode where two LLMs can play Battle Drones against each other A multiplayer mode based on two nearby phones communicating via audio messages, an extension of my earlier experiment with Chirp Pong How I built this Battle Drones is heavily vibe coded - I've reviewed almost none of the code, and it's built in a language (TypeScript) that I've hardly used myself. I've playtested it quite a bit though, and it's been through a large number of iterations since I started the project. Here's a rough history of the project so far, including key prompts and links to transcripts. v1: the initial prototype I started out with Claude Fable 5 back in July: We are going to build a mobile friendly RTS game - command and conquer style - called Battle Drones, in which two armies of drones (both flying and ground-based) battle for territory and resources Let's start with a MVP design, ask me some questions Here's a shared transcript . I'd given Claude Code for Web an environment variable with an OpenAI API key and told it to use the OpenAI Image Generation API for assets, which got me some basic sprites. You can try v1 here - it looked like this: It's recognizable as an RTS, has building mechanics and the ability to select and direct units, and a basic AI to play against. This first version was barely a proof of concept, and it wasn't any fun to play. Claude used the Phaser 2D game framework for these early versions. I didn't even realize this until several iterations later! v2: full sprites The second version ( try v2 here ) added sprites for all of the vehicles and the "AI vs. AI" mode, so I could watch the game playing without having to directly control it myself. Claude proved reasonably competent at prompting OpenAI's image models to generate sprites. You can browse the v2 sprites in the public/assets/sprites folder. v3: varied terrain It still wasn't much fun, and the graphics were boring. It was now October, and I had upgraded to Claude Opus 5.5. I told it: Massively improve this game. Make the graphics and gameplay better (keep it mobile friendly). Render new graphics using the latest OpenAI GPT image API (lookup details) with the API key in the environment variable. Add new unit types and balance the gameplay better. Also add new buildings and better, more varied terrain. This resulted in five new maps with generated background tiles in a variety of styles, visible here . Opus also regenerated the sprites, making them much more visually appealing. You can try v3 here - it looks like this: This is starting to feel like a real game! It still wasn't very fun to play though - I found myself getting bored pretty quickly. v4: the fun update So far my Battle Drones experiment was confirming my previous belief that co

items.rawBody: My obituary for programming Jeremy Scheff poignantly captures the key loss caused by coding agents for career programmers who enjoyed the puzzle of developing code: Programming turned into one of the greatest jobs you could imagine. You got paid to work on tricky little logic puzzles. The trickier the puzzle, the more you got paid. But even pretty simple puzzles were worth a lot of money because regular people just couldn't do it! No, they needed us. They would give us a problem and we would solve it the way we wanted. We set the strategy, we made the timeline, we defined what was and was not possible. If you're a programmer who thrives on building working systems and doesn't care too deeply about the problems solved along the way, LLMs are the gift that keeps on giving. If directly solving those problems was a big part of your enjoyment, the loss is very real. Via lobste.rs Tags: programming , careers , ai , generative-ai , llms , coding-agents , deep-blue

items.rawBody: Release: llm-echo 0.5 I'm working towards a new LLM release, and testing PRs caused me to revisit the llm-echo debug plugin. This plugin provides a "model" which doesn't involve an LLM at all - it just repeats back the prompts that have been fed to it. The new release now updates the simulated token usage counts to take tool calls, system prompts, and reasoning tokens into account. Example usage: uvx --with llm-echo llm -m echo 'hi there' -o thinking 1 --usage Outputs: First I consider the prompt, then I decide what to say. { "prompt": "hi there", "system": "", "attachments": [], "stream": true, "previous": [] } Token usage: 2 input, 24 output Tags: llm

items.titleZh: 【Simon Willison】sparqlite: SPARQL 1.1 inside SQLite, written in Rust

items.rawBody: Research: sparqlite: SPARQL 1.1 inside SQLite, written in Rust This research task is really an experiment in running Claude Code for web in "Ultracode" mode, as described in Orchestrate subagents at scale with dynamic workflows in the Claude Code documentation. With Ultracode turned on, Claude Code makes aggressive use of dynamic workflows - it generates JavaScript that defines and coordinates a network of subagents to take on complex problems. My initial prompt was this - I meant "hit the rows directly", the word "delete" was an accidental typo on my phone: Write a SQLite extension in Rust that implants SPARQL and runs really fast because it can hit the delete rows directly This caused Claude Code for web to churn for over 12 hours. I checked in on its progress the next day and sent a single follow-up prompt when I noticed how many Rust crates it had built: Every folder in the crates/ directory needs a README Include a tutorial.md teaching users how to install the extension and how to run it in the SQLite CLI and then teaching them SPARQL in addition to how to use the SQLite extension Include a script with the tutorial for populating a SQLite database with useful and realistic example data for that tutorial This project feels like next-level vibe coding - it's not remotely feasible to review the code that was produced here, and even following the documentation is a significant investment in work. I'm not entirely sure what to do with this - I appear to have a full SPARQL implementation in Rust inside SQLite now, but how valuable is that if I created it on a whim and can't (or won't) invest the necessary time to understand what it can do? items.bodyText: Some app development platform could come with all the batteries included. Something that looks like the opposite of Vercel Marketplace. Something opinionated, concrete, preconfigured with all the basics that everyone wants: domain, hosting, authentication, payments, database, server functions. If some service made these easy and "just work" out of the box, it could be amazing. For my next app I'm considering rolling with basic HTML/CSS/JS + Python backend (FastAPI + Fly.io style or so?), something a lot simpler than the serverless multiverse of "modern web development". It's possible that a simple app like MenuGen (or apps like it) could have been significantly easier in that paradigm. The companion tweet (and the "comments section") is on my X @karpathy .

items.rawBody: The concept of recursive self-improvement (RSI) dates back to I. J. Good (1965) , where he defined an “ultraintelligent machine” as a system that can surpass humans in all intellectual activities and design better machines to improve itself. Yudkowsky (2008) used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” for a specific feedback loop: an AI uses its current intelligence to improve the cognitive machinery that produces its intelligence. This feedback loop in modern AI may indicate the model rewriting its own weights directly, or more broadly the model improves the training pipeline and the deployment system , which in turn enables a better successor model with improved performance across economically valuable tasks. The speed of research development in AI has been shown to drastically accelerated in frontier labs ( Anthropic ; OpenAI ).

The observation is simple in form: the training loss $L$ decreases predictably as we scale up model size $N$, dataset size $D$, and compute $C$, following a power-law curve, which appears as a straight line on a log-log plot.
